title: How to diagnose OutOfMemoryError — check which area ran out (Heap space, Metaspace, unable to create native thread), take heap dump, analyze for large object retention or memory leaks?

s1_definition.profdef: OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is thrown when the JVM cannot allocate memory and the garbage collector cannot free enough to satisfy the request. The first diagnostic step is reading the error's message to learn which region ran out, because each points to a different cause: "Java heap space" means the heap is exhausted, "Metaspace" means class metadata exhausted, "unable to create new native thread" means the OS could not create another thread, and "GC overhead limit exceeded" means GC is running constantly while freeing almost nothing. You then capture a heap dump and analyze it in Eclipse MAT for large object retention or a leak.
s1_definition.analogy: An OutOfMemoryError at National Bank of India is like a part of the branch becoming completely full so no new work can start. But the message tells you exactly which part. "Heap space" means the main vault is full of objects. "Metaspace" means the office holding the rulebooks is full. "Unable to create native thread" means you tried to hire another teller but there are no desks or badges left in the whole building. Each full room needs a different fix, so the very first thing you do is read the sign on the door that says which room overflowed, and then you photograph that room (heap dump) to see what filled it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Read the OOM message first to learn which region ran out, then take a heap dump and find what is retaining the memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is thrown when the JVM cannot allocate memory and the garbage collector cannot free enough to satisfy the request. The first diagnostic step is reading the error's message to learn which region ran out, because each points to a different cause: "Java heap space" means the heap is exhausted, "Metaspace" means class metadata exhausted, "unable to create new native thread" means the OS could not create another thread, and "GC overhead limit exceeded" means GC is running constantly while freeing almost nothing. You then capture a heap dump and analyze it in Eclipse MAT for large object retention or a leak.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An OutOfMemoryError at National Bank of India is like a part of the branch becoming completely full so no new work can start. But the message tells you exactly which part. "Heap space" means the main vault is full of objects. "Metaspace" means the office holding the rulebooks is full. "Unable to create native thread" means you tried to hire another teller but there are no desks or badges left in the whole building. Each full room needs a different fix, so the very first thing you do is read the sign on the door that says which room overflowed, and then you photograph that room (heap dump) to see what filled it.

**One line to remember:** Read the OOM message first to learn which region ran out, then take a heap dump and find what is retaining the memory.

sections.s2_technical:
The most common variant is `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. It means the heap is full of live objects. The cause is either a genuine need for more memory (undersized `-Xmx`), or a memory leak where objects stay reachable forever, or a spike like loading a huge result set into memory at once. You diagnose it with a heap dump: the Dominator Tree in Eclipse MAT shows which objects retain the most heap, and the path to GC roots shows what holds them.

`OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` means class metadata has filled Metaspace. Since Metaspace holds loaded classes, this usually indicates a class-loading leak: frameworks that generate proxy classes, repeated redeployments in an app server that leak old class loaders, or dynamic scripting that keeps defining classes. You diagnose it by watching loaded-class count climbing over time and by capturing a dump to see which class loaders are retained. The fix is to find what prevents class loaders from being collected, and you bound it with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` so it fails fast.

`OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread` is not about the heap at all. It means the operating system refused to create another thread, usually because the process hit a thread-count or memory limit. Each thread needs a native stack (default around 1MB, set by `-Xss`), so thousands of threads consume real memory outside the heap. The cause is often a thread leak — creating threads without a bounded pool — and the fix is to use a bounded thread pool and check OS ulimits.

`OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded` means the JVM spent over 98 percent of time in GC while recovering less than 2 percent of the heap. It is an early warning of a heap-space problem, treated the same way with a heap dump. A senior nuance: always run production with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and `-XX:HeapDumpPath` so the dump is captured automatically at the moment of failure, and correlate the OOM with GC logs to see whether the heap baseline was drifting up (leak) or spiked suddenly (bad request). You reproduce safely in staging, never debug a leak by just raising `-Xmx`, which only delays the crash.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's reporting service crashed with "Java heap space" after a user requested a report that loaded every transaction for the year into a single list. This is exactly a heap-space OOM from loading too much at once, diagnosed by a heap dump showing one giant list.

Problem 2 — The same service, over weeks of redeployments on the app server, started failing with "Metaspace." This is exactly a class-loader leak, where old class loaders are never collected.

Problem 3 — A batch job that spawned a new thread per account instead of using a pool failed with "unable to create new native thread." This is exactly a thread leak, unrelated to the heap.

Our mini-project builds an `OomDiagnosticsDemo` that can trigger each OOM variant on demand and an `OomClassifier` that reads the thrown error's message and prints the likely cause and the correct next step, teaching the reader to triage by region. Heap dump on OOM is enabled so a `.hprof` is produced for the heap-space case.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-oom-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── OomDiagnosticsDemo.java    (main runnable demo)
            ├── ReportService.java         (triggers heap-space OOM)
            └── OomClassifier.java         (reads message, prints cause + fix)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Heap-space OOM with automatic heap dump for MAT analysis
java -Xms64m -Xmx64m \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/bank-heap-oom.hprof \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.OomDiagnosticsDemo heap

# Thread-exhaustion OOM (small stacks make it faster to hit; be careful on shared hosts)
java -Xss256k -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.OomDiagnosticsDemo thread

# Inspect what region is exhausted on a live process
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary    # requires -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
jstack <pid> | grep -c '"'              # count live threads

# Then analyze the .hprof in Eclipse MAT: Dominator Tree + Leak Suspects + Path to GC Roots
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the launch mode ("heap" or "thread"), a 64MB heap cap for the heap case, and heap-dump-on-OOM enabled.

Step 1 — In heap mode, the ReportService loads 1MB "transaction batch" arrays into a list without bound, simulating a request that tries to pull a whole year of data into memory at once.

Step 2 — The list grows past what the 64MB heap can hold. GC runs but cannot free the arrays because the list keeps strong references to all of them. The JVM throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

Step 3 — Because `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` is set, the JVM first writes `bank-heap-oom.hprof` capturing the entire heap at the moment of failure.

Step 4 — The OomClassifier catches the error, reads its message, recognizes "Java heap space," and logs the cause (leak or over-loading) and the next step (analyze the dump in MAT).

Step 5 — In thread mode instead, the code spawns threads forever. Each needs a native stack outside the heap. The OS eventually refuses, and the JVM throws "unable to create new native thread." The classifier recognizes this and points to a bounded thread pool and OS ulimits, not the heap.

Step 6 — The engineer opens the heap dump in Eclipse MAT. The Dominator Tree shows a single ArrayList retaining nearly the whole heap full of 1MB arrays, confirming "loading too much at once." The fix is to stream and paginate the report instead of loading everything.

Final output (heap mode):

```
2026-10-31 23:19:00 [INFO] Loading full-year report for CUR3001 (loads everything into memory)
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Dumping heap to /tmp/bank-heap-oom.hprof ...
2026-10-31 23:19:01 [SEVERE] OutOfMemoryError caught: Java heap space
2026-10-31 23:19:01 [SEVERE] CAUSE: heap exhausted (leak OR loading too much at once).
2026-10-31 23:19:01 [SEVERE] NEXT: analyze the auto heap dump in Eclipse MAT -> Dominator Tree.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I hit an OutOfMemoryError, the very first thing I do is read the error message, because it tells me which region of memory ran out, and each region points to a completely different cause and fix. If it says "Java heap space," the heap is full of live objects, which means either a genuine need for a bigger heap, a memory leak, or a request that tried to load far too much into memory at once. If it says "Metaspace," class metadata is exhausted, which almost always means a class-loader leak from things like proxy generation or repeated redeployments. If it says "unable to create new native thread," it is not a heap problem at all; the operating system refused another thread, usually because of a thread leak or an OS limit, since every thread needs a native stack outside the heap. And "GC overhead limit exceeded" is an early warning of a heap problem, where GC is running almost constantly while freeing almost nothing.

Once I know the region, I take a heap dump and analyze it. In production I always run with heap-dump-on-OutOfMemoryError and a dump path set, so the JVM captures a full snapshot at the exact moment of failure instead of losing the evidence. I open that dump in Eclipse Memory Analyzer, where the Dominator Tree shows which objects retain the most memory and the path to GC roots shows exactly what is holding them alive. I also correlate with the GC logs to tell whether the heap baseline was drifting up slowly, which signals a leak, or spiked suddenly, which signals a bad request.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I have diagnosed all three of these. Our reporting service crashed with "Java heap space" because a report tried to load an entire year of transactions into one list, and the heap dump made it obvious with a single giant list dominating memory, so we fixed it by streaming and paginating instead. On the same app server, after many redeployments, we hit "Metaspace" from leaked class loaders, which we bounded with MaxMetaspaceSize so it failed fast and alerted. And a batch job that spawned a thread per account instead of using a pool failed with "unable to create new native thread," which we fixed with a bounded thread pool. The habit that saves me every time is to read the message first and never just raise the heap size, because that only delays a leak instead of fixing it.

---

keyPoints: Heap OOM: capture heap dump, analyze with MAT, find leak
Metaspace OOM: too many classes loaded — check classloader leaks
Direct buffer OOM: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, check NIO buffer usage
GC overhead limit: GC spending >98% time recovering <2% memory
Stack OOM: too many threads — reduce thread count or increase -Xss
